'''Friedrich Heinrich Helmut Lieth''' ({{Birth date|1925|12|16|df=y}}{{Spaced en dash space}}{{Death date|2015|4|16|df=y}}) was a German [[Ecology|ecologist]], [[Botany|botanist]] and [[Phytogeography|phytogeographer]].<ref name="Biog">{{cite journal |first=Marina |last=Mochtchenko |url=http://www.tropecol.com/pdf/open/PDF_45_1/45101.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160106212414/http://www.tropecol.com/pdf/open/PDF_45_1/45101.pdf |url-status=usurped |archive-date=January 6, 2016 |title=Prof. Dr. em. Helmut Lieth: The man and his life for global ecology |journal=[[Tropical Ecology]] |volume=45 |date=2004 |pages=1&ndash;2}}</ref><ref name="DNB">{{DNB-Portal|105031402}}</ref>

==Biography==
Lieth received his doctorate in Biology from the [[University of Cologne]] in 1953 and became a private lecturer at the [[University of Hohenheim|University of Stuttgart-Hohenheim]] in 1960. He was then a visiting professor in [[Venezuela]], [[Colombia]], and in 1966 at the [[University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa|University of Hawaii]]. He was professor at the [[University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill]] from 1967 to 1977. From then until 1992 he was a professor at the [[University of Osnabrück]] where he held the chair of ecology.<ref name="CV">{{cite web |url=http://www.usf.uos.de/~hlieth |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050406042840/http://www.usf.uos.de/~hlieth |title=USF + AppSysSc: Homepage of Helmut Lieth |archivedate=6 April 2005}}</ref>

Helmut Lieth married Magdalena Roth in 1952.<ref name="CV" /> The couple had a daughter (Dr. Margot Lieth) and three sons (Prof. Dr. Johann Heinrich Lieth, Dr. Erich Lieth and Armin Lieth); he also had a daughter (Masha) from a second marriage to Marina Mochtchenko.

==Research==
Lieth became widely known through the ''climate diagram world atlas'' published together with [[Heinrich Walter]] between 1960 and 1967. The descriptive form of climate display (the Walter-Lieth climate diagram ) conceived here received the highest international recognition.

His work on use of geospatial mapping (Lieth 1974, 1975) resulted in many computer-generated maps and was the pioneering work that is today commonly referred to as Graphical Information Systems (GIS).
